summary.summary: Oxfordshire took no new borrowing in 2025/26 and let £7m of debt go (a £2m PWLB maturity plus a £5m LOBO its lender called in November 2025), leaving £264.8m of borrowing against a £512.5m capital financing requirement — 48% internally funded — alongside £424m of investments. Treasury income beat budget by £8.2m on higher rates and balances, and the council parked the gains in reserves, including £8.0m added to a High Needs DSG risk reserve in June 2026. The shadow is the schools grant: the negative High Needs DSG balance reached £149.3m by year end, costing an estimated £6.0m in unearned interest this year (£16.4m cumulative since 2019/20) and steadily eating the cash the council can invest.

signals.headline: Negative High Needs DSG balance reached £149.3m by 31 March 2026; estimated £6.0m of unearned interest cost in 2025/26 (up from £3.8m in 2024/25), £16.4m cumulative since 2019/20
signals.why: The deficit behind the statutory override is consuming investable cash at an accelerating rate, and the council is pre-emptively parking £8m of treasury gains in a High Needs risk reserve against it.

signals.headline: A £5m LOBO at 3.68% was called and repaid without penalty on 24 November 2025; four LOBO loans totalling £20m remain
signals.why: Lenders have started exercising their options in this rate environment; the remaining £20m is modest against £424m of investments, so a further call is manageable.

signals.headline: No new external borrowing in 2025/26; debt down from £271.9m to £264.8m against a £512.5m CFR, with internal balances funding 48% of the requirement
signals.why: Shrinking external debt plus £424m of investments leaves little refinancing exposure — only 12.16% of borrowing matures within 12 months against a 20% limit.

news_drafts.headline: Oxfordshire's money set aside for named purposes falls £16.2m to £163.8m as capital schemes draw on it
news_drafts.lead:
Oxfordshire County Council's money set aside for named purposes (earmarked reserves) stands at £163.8m, which is £16.2m lower than the £180.0m in the capital programme it approved. The figures are in a capital programme update going to the council's Cabinet on 20 October 2026. The capital programme is the council's planned spending on things that last, such as buildings and roads.

The report, a monitoring paper dated August 2026, says the reduction comes from releasing provisions to the capital improvements it sets out. These include £3.3m for Bus Service Improvement funding and £2.3m for residential accommodation. In the paper's words, "The level of earmarked reserves has decreased by £ 16.2m".

Of the £163.8m that remains, £37.9m is budget provisions and £125.9m is other provisions.
news_drafts.paper_title: CA201026R15 Capital Programme Update Monitoring Report Aug 2026 (Cabinet Oct 26)

news_drafts.headline: Oxfordshire's audit recovery stalls into third year after disclaimed opinion
news_drafts.lead: Oxfordshire County Council remains locked in multi-year audit recovery, with its accounts still unable to receive an unqualified sign-off three years after a complete audit failure. The auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion in 2023/24—the most serious form of audit failure—and a qualified opinion last year. Even by 2025/26, certain valuations and reserve movements will still lack assurance. The auditors have now flagged the council's General Fund Balance, a key measure of financial resilience, as presenting higher inherent risk due to material unaudited movements and susceptibility to management bias. They require confirmation that management can simultaneously rebuild historic records from 2022/23 onwards while delivering current-year audit work, and have signalled they will seek additional audit fees to reflect the scope of extra work required. Recovery remains on track for an unqualified opinion by 2026/27, but the pattern suggests underlying capacity constraints.

findings.headline: Pipeline schemes are shown at £37,908k in total, down £17,459k from £55,367k, with the 2026/27 figure cut from £8,165k to £200k.
findings.detail: The pipeline line is indicative funding subject to initial business case, so these figures are not committed. The paper does not explain the reduction in the cover material above the figures.
findings.matters: Pipeline schemes show what a council intends to build beyond its approved programme, so a reduction shows the pipeline has shrunk, whatever the cause.
findings.figures: Pipeline 2026/27 original 8,165, latest 200, variation -7,965; total original 55,367, latest 37,908, variation -17,459 (£'000s)

findings.headline: Use of capital reserves is shown as a funding source of £88,536k, with £51,063k in 2029/30 and £25,787k in the period up to 2035/36.
findings.detail: The sources table shows capital reserves being drawn from 2029/30 onward, with no draw in the earlier years. The capital reserve carry-forward row shows the balance falling from 88,536 to 25,787 over the same period.
findings.matters: A council drawing down capital reserves to fund the programme in later years leaves less headroom, which is relevant to anyone assessing its funding position.
findings.figures: Use of capital reserves 0, 0, 0, 51,063, 11,686, 25,787; total 88,536. Capital reserve c/fwd 88,536 (2028/29) to 25,787 (up to 2035/36) (£'000s)

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing is shown as a funding source of £206,415k across 2026/27 to 2035/36, with £75,452k in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The sources of funding table shows prudential borrowing by year, with the largest amounts in 2026/27 and 2028/29. The figure is one of several sources, alongside grants, developer contributions and capital receipts.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would want to see the scale of new borrowing the programme depends on, and when it falls.

findings.headline: Actual capital expenditure to date is £115,279k, 26% of the 2026/27 programme, with commitments taking the figure to 44%.
findings.detail: The paper reports the realisation rate for the total capital programme for 2026/27 as 26%, and actuals plus commitments as 44%. Expenditure to date is 115,279 and commitments are 76,844, against a latest current-year forecast of 436,007.
findings.matters: Spend to date against the year's forecast shows how far the programme is running ahead of or behind its profile at the half-year point.
findings.figures: Actual to date 115,279; commitments 76,844; realisation 26%; actuals and commitments 44%; latest current-year forecast 436,007 (£'000s)

findings.headline: Property Strategy's 2026/27 forecast is £73,438k, up £37,888k (107%) from the £35,550k in the May 2026 Cabinet report.
findings.detail: Against the February 2026 original of 70,942, the current-year forecast is up 2,496. Actual expenditure to date is 38,295, which is 52% of the latest forecast, with commitments of 7,343.
findings.matters: A forecast that more than doubles within one cycle is a large change in the timing of property spend and the funding that goes with it.
findings.figures: Current year 73,438 (latest) vs 70,942 (original) vs 35,550 (May 2026); variation +2,496 vs original, +37,888 vs May (107%); actual to date 38,295; commitments 7,343; realisation 52% (£'000s)
